stimulus.text:
“Our very first Christmas at Hull House, when we as yet knew nothing of child labor, a number of little girls refused the candy which was offered them as part of the Christmas good cheer, saying simply that they “worked in a candy factory and could not bear the sight of it.” We discovered that for six weeks they had worked from seven in the morning until nine at night, and they were exhausted as well as satiated.”

Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910), Chapter X, describing Christmas 1889.
stimulus.source_note: Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910), Chapter X. Public domain; text checked against the University of Pennsylvania digital edition.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)

books.section: Topic 6.8 Immigration and Migration in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910), Chapter X

stem: The girls worked from seven in the morning until nine at night for six weeks. That detail best supports which claim about immigrant children in the Gilded Age?

options.text: Many immigrant children worked long hours, and their families needed their wages
Chicago factories refused to hire immigrant children
options.misconception: Denies hiring that the passage proves happened.

options.text: Hull House paid the girls to work in its candy factory
options.misconception: Confuses the settlement house with the factory.

options.text: Child labor laws had already ended factory work for children by 1889
options.misconception: Claims a law ended work that was plainly going on.

rationales.A: Fourteen-hour days for six weeks show children carrying factory work, and Addams writes that such children’s earnings supported their parents.
rationales.B: The girls did work in the factory. The factories hired them.
rationales.C: Hull House did not pay the girls. A candy factory employed them.
rationales.D: The girls were working in 1889, so no law had yet ended their factory work.
rationales.general:
Read the hours, then ask what they meant for a family.
1. Seven in the morning until nine at night is fourteen hours a day.
2. Six weeks of such days left the girls exhausted.
3. Children worked such hours because their families needed the pay.
4. Long hours plus family need is the pattern, not a single accident.
Background: Addams writes that working children contributed to the support of their parents.
Remember: hours tell you the work; family need tells you why children did it.
